title: Is Your School Lying To You?
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin describes a demoralizing 'lie' whispered to teachers in the toughest schools: that their students are simply too far gone to reach. He attributes this false belief not to the students but to a permissive, low-standard school culture that treats minor test-score gains as victories while tolerating chronic disorder. He insists teachers retain control within their own classroom regardless of broader school dysfunction, and lays out three keys to building a countervailing classroom culture: slowing everything down to restore seriousness and purpose, requiring students to demonstrably prove they've learned every expectation and lesson, and enforcing consistent consequences for anyone who disrupts that process. He closes by directing readers to SCM's books and archive as tools for sustained implementation.
points: Identifies a demoralizing 'lie'—that certain students are too far gone—as originating from school culture, not the students themselves.
Argues low institutional standards, not student capability, are the true source of chronic classroom chaos.
Recommends slowing everything down and modeling even trivial routines to the highest standard as the first step to change.
Advises requiring students to prove they've learned material through demonstrable performance, not passive compliance.
Insists teachers retain full control within their own classroom regardless of the broader school's dysfunction.
quotes: It says, “Your students can’t do it.” It tells them that the situation is hopeless, that their students are too far gone, so shaped and bent by bad influences that the good doesn’t stand a chance.
It’s a systemic failure that views a 1% improvement in abysmal reading scores as something to crow about.
You, after all, control the world within your classroom—at least, in a classroom management sense. Yes, it’s difficult when chaos runs roughshod over everything around you.
So move slower, speak deliberately and less frequently, and pause often. In between, teach and model every little detail you want your students to do or to know to the highest standard.

As such, you must require your students to prove to you they understand and have learned well the content of your lessons by doing, performing, or otherwise mirroring back to you what you’ve taught them.
If you invest the time to learn our approach, no school on earth can stop you from creating an oasis of truth and excellence in what may very well be a vast desert of dysfunction and disarray.
